title: America Online, swamped by its own success, can now be bought
what: Shares of America Online of Dulles, Virginia, the biggest online service with more than 8 million members, can be bought from this month; it moved its listing from the Nasdaq to the New York Stock Exchange in September. In December it began charging a flat $19.95 a month for unlimited use, and its network jammed: members met busy signals for hours. On 29 January it settled with 36 states, offering refunds of up to $39.90, halting most advertising in February and promising $160 million of new equipment. Buyers bet that America Online will become the main way households go online.
why: The listing beat. AOL was at a low point (its share had fallen far from its 1996 high), and the flat rate that caused the busy signals was the price that made it the internet's mass-market door.
source: https://money.cnn.com/1997/01/29/technology/aol/ (CNNfn, 29 January 1997, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1997/02/03/technology/aol/ (CNNfn, 3 February 1997, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1996/09/16/technology/case_intv/ (CNNfn, 16 September 1996, on the move to the NYSE, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL raises its price, and its shares hit a high
what: On 9 February America Online said it will raise its unlimited monthly fee by 10%, to $21.95, from April. Its members now spend 23 hours a month online on average, against 7 hours before the flat rate, and every minute costs AOL money. Its shares jumped to a 52-week high on the news. AOL also cut 500 jobs at CompuServe, the rival online service it has just acquired, and made Robert Pittman president and chief executive of America Online, with founder Steve Case remaining chairman.
why: Pricing power proved: +27% in February 1998.
source: https://money.cnn.com/1998/02/09/technology/aol/ (CNNfn, 9 February 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1998/01/30/technology/aol/ (CNNfn, 30 January 1998, on the CompuServe purchase, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL pays $287 million for ICQ, a free chat program
what: America Online announced on 8 June that it has bought Mirabilis, an Israeli company whose free program ICQ tells users when their friends are online and lets them exchange messages instantly. AOL paid $287 million in cash and may pay up to $120 million more over three years if ICQ meets growth targets. ICQ, launched in November 1996, will stay a free service based in Tel Aviv with its own brand.
why: AOL buying audience, as it would with Netscape: +27% in June 1998, in a strong month for internet shares.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000883780/000088378098000023/0000883780-98-000023.txt (America Online 8-K of June 1998, read 2026-10-14);

title: Good results do not save AOL's shares from the August slump
what: America Online reported on 4 August results for its fiscal year to June that beat Wall Street's forecasts, and said it was comfortable with analysts' estimates for the coming year. Internet shares rallied for a few days. But August turned into a bad month for the stock market: by its end the Dow Jones index had fallen more than 18% from its July record amid crises in several countries. Internet shares are 'high beta, high risk stocks,' said one analyst. 'They seem to overreact to whichever direction the market is in.'
why: A market move: -30% in August 1998 against -15% for the market.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000883780/000088378098000039/0000883780-98-000039.txt (America Online 8-K of 4 August 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1998/08/07/markets/internet/ (CNNfn, 7 August 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1998/09/08/markets/marketwrap/ (CNNfn, 8 September 1998, read 2026-10-14)

title: Hopes of a rate cut bring internet shares roaring back
what: On 4 September Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan said the American economy could not remain untouched while the rest of the world slows down. Investors took it as a hint that interest rates may be cut, and on 8 September the Dow Jones index rose 380 points, its biggest one-day gain ever. Internet shares, the market's most volatile, rebounded hardest after their sharp fall, and America Online's shares were among the biggest gainers.
why: The rebound from the August sell-off: +36% in September 1998 against +6% for the market.
source: https://money.cnn.com/1998/09/08/markets/marketwrap/ (CNNfn, 8 September 1998, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL buys Netscape and teams up with Sun
what: America Online, with 14 million subscribers, agreed on 24 November to buy Netscape for shares worth $4.2 billion, gaining the Navigator browser and Netcenter, one of the ten most-visited web sites. In a separate three-year alliance, AOL will buy $500 million of computers and services from Sun Microsystems, and Sun will pay AOL more than $350 million in licence, marketing and advertising fees. AOL will keep shipping Microsoft's Internet Explorer with its software. Its shares rose on the news.
why: AOL as the internet's consolidator: +38% in November 1998.
source: https://money.cnn.com/1998/11/24/technology/aol/ (CNNfn, 24 November 1998, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL joins the S&P 500 and its shares soar
what: On 22 December Standard & Poor's said America Online will join its index of 500 leading American shares, replacing Venator, the former Woolworth's. AOL's shares jumped more than 13% in trading after the close, and Deutsche Bank raised its price target the next morning. Funds that track the index must now buy the shares. AOL was worth about $41 billion at the time, making it one of the most valuable companies on the New York Stock Exchange; the new member gives the old index a technology slant.
why: The best month in AOL's game life: +83% in December 1998, at the height of the internet rally.
source: https://money.cnn.com/1998/12/22/markets/afterbell/ (CNNfn, 22 December 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1998/12/23/companies/aol/ (CNNfn, 23 December 1998, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL passes 18 million members and beats forecasts
what: America Online reported on 20 October a profit of $184 million, or 15 cents a share, for its first fiscal quarter, against 13 cents expected by analysts. Revenue rose 47% to $1.5 billion, and advertising and commerce revenue doubled to $350 million. The service gained 1.1 million members in the quarter and now has more than 18 million worldwide. AOL also agreed with the computer maker Gateway to put its service on Gateway's PCs and to run Gateway's internet service.
why: Growth still beating forecasts: +25% in October 1999.
source: https://money.cnn.com/1999/10/20/news/aol/ (CNNfn, 20 October 1999, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL Time Warner is born
what: America Online and Time Warner completed their merger on 11 January, after the Federal Communications Commission approved it with conditions: AOL must open its cable lines to rival internet providers and let other services talk to its instant messaging. The new AOL Time Warner, owner of the AOL service, CNN, HBO, Time magazine and the Warner Bros. studio, trades under the symbol AOL. Each America Online share became one AOL Time Warner share; Time Warner holders got 1.5. Chief executive Gerald Levin expects revenue above $40 billion this year, growing 12 to 15% a year. The shares had risen sharply in the first days of January in anticipation.
why: The merger closed a year after it was announced (tech 1f8b5752), as the internet bust was well under way: +51% in January 2001, a relief rally on approval.
source: https://money.cnn.com/2001/01/11/deals/hold_aol/ (CNNfn, 11 January 2001, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/2001/01/12/deals/new_aol/ (CNNfn, 12 January 2001, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL Time Warner beats forecasts on the day of a surprise rate cut
what: AOL Time Warner reported on 18 April first-quarter earnings that were better than Wall Street expected. The same morning the Federal Reserve surprised the market with its fourth interest-rate cut of the year, half a percentage point, a month before its next meeting. The Nasdaq index jumped 8.1%, one of its biggest daily gains, and AOL Time Warner's shares rose $5.10 to $49.
why: A rebound from the winter's lows: +26% in April 2001 against +8% for the market.
source: https://money.cnn.com/2001/04/18/markets/markets_newyork/ (CNNfn, 18 April 2001, read 2026-10-14); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001105705/000095015701500021/aol-8k.txt (AOL Time Warner 8-K of 18 April 2001, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL Time Warner loses $54 billion in a quarter
what: AOL Time Warner reported on 24 April a net loss of $54.2 billion for the first quarter, one of the biggest in corporate history, almost all of it a one-time charge for the fall in value of the businesses combined in the merger, booked under a new accounting rule. Revenue rose 4% to $9.8 billion. Richard Parsons, who becomes chief executive next month when Gerald Levin retires, cut the year's profit growth target and blamed weak online advertising at America Online. The shares closed at $19.30.
why: The merger's failure in numbers: the write-down admitted that AOL had paid with overvalued shares.
source: https://money.cnn.com/2002/04/24/technology/aol/ (CNN/Money, 24 April 2002, read 2026-10-14)

title: Pittman leaves, and the SEC looks at AOL's accounts
what: On 18 July Robert Pittman, who came from America Online, resigned as chief operating officer of AOL Time Warner, giving more power to two Time Warner executives, Don Logan of Time Inc. and Jeff Bewkes of HBO. The same day the Washington Post reported that AOL had booked more than $270 million of questionable advertising revenue in 2000 and 2001 through swaps with partners. On 24 July chief executive Richard Parsons said the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into the company's accounting. The shares fell to their lowest since August 1998.
why: The Time Warner side took control; the accounting questions led to the 2004/2005 settlements.
source: https://money.cnn.com/2002/07/18/news/aol/index.htm (CNN/Money, 18 July 2002, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/2002/07/24/technology/aol/index.htm (CNN/Money, 24 July 2002, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/2002/07/25/technology/aol/index.htm (CNN/Money, 25 July 2002, read 2026-10-14)

title: A $99 billion loss, and Steve Case steps down
what: Steve Case, the founder of America Online who engineered the purchase of Time Warner, said on 12 January he will give up the chairmanship in May, as shareholders blame him for the merger. On 29 January AOL Time Warner reported a fourth-quarter loss of $44.9 billion, again mostly a write-down of America Online, bringing its loss for 2002 to about $99 billion, the biggest ever for an American company. Vice chairman Ted Turner, its largest shareholder, is also stepping down. The shares have fallen about 80% since the merger was announced.
why: The last of the AOL founders left the top; the record loss was the second write-down of the merger.
source: https://money.cnn.com/2003/01/12/news/companies/aol/index.htm (CNN/Money, 13 January 2003, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/2003/01/29/technology/aol/index.htm (CNN/Money, 29 January 2003, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL Time Warner becomes Time Warner again
what: On 16 October AOL Time Warner officially dropped 'AOL' from its name, after its board voted for the change in September. The company is now Time Warner, its shares trade under the old Time Warner symbol TWX instead of AOL, and its new headquarters at Columbus Circle in Manhattan will be called the Time Warner Center. Chief executive Richard Parsons said the name better reflects the range of its businesses, from film studios and cable television to magazines and America Online, and ends confusion with the AOL brand.
why: The rename beat: the internet company that had bought Time Warner became a division of it.
source: https://money.cnn.com/2003/09/18/technology/aol_name/ (CNN/Money, 18 September 2003, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/2003/10/16/technology/timewarner_name/ (CNN/Money, 16 October 2003, read 2026-10-14)

title: Time Warner settles the AOL accounting investigations
what: Time Warner announced on 15 December that it has settled the Justice Department's investigation of America Online's dealings with PurchasePro.com: prosecution of AOL is deferred for two years, and the company pays a $60 million penalty and sets up a $150 million fund for shareholder lawsuits. It also proposed a settlement to the Securities and Exchange Commission: a $300 million penalty, and corrected accounts for about $400 million of advertising revenue booked mainly in 2001 and 2002 in deals with Bertelsmann.
why: The bill for the advertising deals of the bubble years. The SEC approved the settlement on 21 March 2005.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001105705/000110570504000051/f04-12_158kex991.txt (Time Warner press release of 15 December 2004, read 2026-10-14); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001105705/000110570505000024/f05-03_218kex991.txt (Time Warner press release of 21 March 2005, read 2026-10-14)

title: Google pays $1 billion for 5% of AOL
what: Google and Time Warner announced on 20 December that Google will invest $1 billion for a 5% stake in America Online and expand their partnership: Google will sell advertising across AOL's sites, more AOL content will appear for Google's users, and Google's chat program will talk to AOL's instant messenger. AOL brought Google 10% of its revenue in the third quarter, and had also talked with Microsoft's MSN.
why: AOL reinvented as an advertising business, with Google's money and search.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001105705/000110570505000047/f05-12_21ex992.txt (joint press release of 20 December 2005, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/2005/12/16/technology/aol_talks/index.htm (CNN/Money, 16 December 2005, read 2026-10-14)

title: Time Warner settles with Carl Icahn: a $20 billion buyback
what: Time Warner reached an agreement on 17 February with Icahn Partners, the group of shareholders led by the investor Carl Icahn, who had warned the company not to sell AOL cheaply and had threatened to contest the board. Icahn will not contest the board at the 2006 annual meeting. In return Time Warner will raise its share buyback to $20 billion through 2007, about $15 billion of it by the end of 2006, add two independent directors, and keep studying the proposals of a report by the bank Lazard.
why: The activist campaign of 2005/2006 ended in a buyback rather than a break-up.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1105705/000110570506000016/0001105705-06-000016.txt (Time Warner statement of 17 February 2006, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/2005/12/16/technology/aol_talks/index.htm (CNN/Money, 16 December 2005, on Icahn's warning, read 2026-10-14)

title: AOL becomes free
what: Time Warner announced on 2 August that AOL will let anyone with an internet connection use most of its services, including its software and an AOL e-mail account, without charge; only dial-up access will still cost money. AOL's members have been leaving for faster broadband lines, and in the second quarter its subscription revenue fell 11% while its advertising revenue rose 40%. The plan is to keep former subscribers as readers of AOL's sites and earn money from advertising.
why: The end of the subscription model that built AOL.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001105705/000095014406007215/g02601exv99w1.htm (Time Warner second-quarter release of 2 August 2006, read 2026-10-14); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001105705/000095014406010008/g03742e10vq.htm (Time Warner 10-Q for the third quarter of 2006, describing the strategy announced on 2 August, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/2006/09/13/news/companies/aol/index.htm (CNNMoney, 13 September 2006, read 2026-10-14)

title: Jeff Bewkes takes over Time Warner
what: Jeffrey Bewkes, the former head of HBO, became chief executive of Time Warner on 1 January, succeeding Richard Parsons, who stays on as chairman; the change was announced in November. Time Warner owns the Warner Bros. studio, CNN, HBO, AOL and most of Time Warner Cable. Its shares, at about $18 when the change was announced, were roughly where they stood when Parsons took over in May 2002, and have lagged those of Disney and News Corp.
why: Bewkes went on to take the group apart: Time Warner Cable in 2009, AOL at the end of 2009.
source: https://money.cnn.com/2007/11/05/news/companies/twx_parsons_bewkes/ (CNNMoney, 5 November 2007, read 2026-10-14)

title: Time Warner spins off its cable business and merges its shares three into one
what: Time Warner separated Time Warner Cable on 12 March and began handing its cable shares to its own shareholders on 27 March: 0.083670 Time Warner Cable share for each Time Warner share held on 12 March. The same evening it merged every three of its own shares into one. A holder of 300 Time Warner shares thus now owns 100 new Time Warner shares and about 25 Time Warner Cable shares; fractions are paid in cash. Chief executive Jeff Bewkes says Time Warner is now one of the leading pure content companies.
why: The first step in undoing the AOL Time Warner merger. For the game's price series: the spun-off cable shares are value paid out to holders, and the reverse split changes the share basis.
source: https://investors.att.com/~/media/Files/A/ATT-IR-V2/time-warner-documents/time-warner-cable-separation-information/final-twx-twc-separationfinalpr-032709.pdf (Time Warner press release of 27 March 2009, read 2026-10-14); https://investors.att.com/stockholder-services/time-warner-stockholders/time-warner-cable-separation/how-many-shares-of-time-warner-cable-common-stock-did-time-warner-stockholders-receive (read 2026-10-14)

title: Time Warner lets AOL go
what: Time Warner completed the spin-off of AOL on 9 December: for every eleven Time Warner shares held on 27 November, shareholders received one share of AOL, which again trades on its own on the New York Stock Exchange. The marriage formed in January 2001 is over; Time Warner, now a film, television and publishing company, says it has returned to its roots. In this game the Time Warner share leaves the market here: holders are paid out in cash at the November 2009 price.
why: The exit beat. From the 2001 merger to the split, the shares lost most of their value; the game ends the series here.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001105705/000095015709000979/ex99-1.htm (Time Warner press release of 10 December 2009, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/2009/05/28/technology/timewarner_aol/ (CNNMoney, 28 May 2009, read 2026-10-14)
